description: Patterns of population change and the impact of migration on UK communities.
content_html:
What Is Migration?

Migration is the movement of people from one place to another. It can be internal — within a country, such as people moving from rural areas to cities — or international, meaning movement across national borders. Immigrants are people who move into a country, while emigrants are those who leave. The difference between the number arriving and the number leaving is called net migration. When more people arrive than leave, net migration is positive; when more leave than arrive, it is negative.

A Brief History of Migration to the UK

The UK has a long history as both a destination for migrants and a source of emigrants. In earlier centuries, waves of Huguenot refugees from France, Jewish communities fleeing persecution in Eastern Europe, and Irish workers seeking employment all contributed to the population. After the Second World War, the British government actively recruited workers from the Caribbean, South Asia and elsewhere to help rebuild the economy and staff the newly created NHS. The Windrush generation — named after the ship HMT Empire Windrush, which arrived at Tilbury in 1948 — became a defining part of British multicultural history.

From the 1990s onwards, migration from European Union member states increased significantly, particularly after 2004 when eight Eastern European countries joined the EU and their citizens gained the right to live and work in the UK under EU free movement rules. Following the UK’s departure from the EU in January 2020, freedom of movement between the UK and EU member states ended. A new points-based immigration system was introduced that applies equally to EU and non-EU citizens seeking to live and work in the UK.

Key Fact

When the UK left the EU in January 2020, freedom of movement between the UK and EU member states ended. A points-based immigration system now applies to both EU and non-EU citizens seeking to work in the UK.

Why Do People Migrate?

Geographers and social scientists use the terms “push factors” and “pull factors” to explain why people move. Push factors are conditions that make people want to leave a place — for example, conflict, poverty, political persecution, environmental disasters or lack of employment. Pull factors are conditions that attract people to a particular destination — such as higher wages, political safety, better public services, an established community of people from the same background, or family connections.

It is important to distinguish between voluntary migration (people who choose to move, typically for economic or personal reasons) and forced migration. A refugee is someone who has been forced to flee their country because of a well-founded fear of persecution on grounds such as race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership of a particular social group. An asylum seeker is someone who has applied for refugee status but whose application has not yet been decided. Asylum seekers are not the same as illegal immigrants; applying for asylum is a legal right under international law, established by the 1951 UN Refugee Convention.

Key Fact

A refugee has been granted protection after fleeing persecution. An asylum seeker has applied for refugee status and is awaiting a decision. Applying for asylum is a legal right under the 1951 UN Refugee Convention.

Supporters of immigration argue that it brings significant economic, cultural and social benefits. Economically, migrants often fill skills shortages in key sectors: the NHS, social care, construction and agriculture all rely substantially on migrant workers. Many economists argue that migrants contribute more in taxes and public spending than they receive in services, particularly in their working years. Culturally, immigration has enriched British food, music, art, science and sport. Demographically, immigration helps offset an ageing population by bringing in younger workers who support public pension and healthcare systems.

Critics of high levels of immigration argue that rapid population change can put pressure on public services such as schools, housing and GP surgeries, particularly in areas that receive the highest concentration of new arrivals. Some argue that unchecked immigration can suppress wages for low-paid workers in sectors where labour supply is abundant. Others raise concerns about integration: if migration is very rapid, they argue, it can be harder for communities to build the shared understanding and civic ties that make a diverse society function well. These concerns apply particularly to debates about policy, not to individuals or communities themselves. Examiners expect students to present both perspectives without dismissing either.

The Impact of Migration on UK Communities

Migration has shaped and continues to shape the UK in visible ways. Many areas of the UK have substantial communities with heritage from South Asia, the Caribbean, West Africa, Eastern Europe and the Middle East. These communities have built places of worship, businesses, cultural organisations and community networks that are part of local life. Languages, foods and festivals that originated elsewhere are now part of everyday British culture.

At the same time, migration has also raised questions about housing, labour markets and public services in specific areas. Local authorities in areas of high migration have at times reported pressure on school places, social housing and healthcare. These are policy and resource questions, not inherent consequences of migration itself — they reflect whether government investment in public services has kept pace with population growth.

Students sometimes use the terms “refugee,” “asylum seeker” and “economic migrant” interchangeably. These are legally distinct categories with different rights and obligations. An economic migrant moves voluntarily in search of better living standards. An asylum seeker is seeking legal protection because they claim to have fled persecution — their claim is assessed under international law. A refugee is someone whose claim has been accepted. Mixing up these terms in exam answers is penalised because it shows imprecise use of citizenship terminology. Use the correct term for the group you are discussing.

Migration and Citizenship Values

Questions about migration sit at the intersection of several core citizenship values: human rights (including the right to seek asylum), national sovereignty (the right of a democratic state to control its own borders), equality (treating all people with dignity regardless of their origins) and social cohesion (building a shared civic society). How to balance these values is one of the most contested political debates in contemporary democracies. As a citizenship student, your task is to understand the different perspectives, use the correct terminology and present a balanced argument — not to take a personal political position.
exam_tip_html: Migration is one of the most politically contested topics in citizenship. On any extended-response question about immigration, make sure you present at least two clearly distinct viewpoints and that neither side is caricatured or dismissed. The most common error is producing an answer that reads as a personal opinion rather than a balanced analysis. For 8-mark and 12-mark questions, naming a specific law or agreement (such as the 1951 UN Refugee Convention, the Equality Act 2010, or the points-based immigration system introduced after 2020) will lift your answer into the Secure or Mastering band. For source interpretation questions on this topic, avoid simply summarising the source — reach a judgement about what it shows, link it to your own knowledge, and state what it tells us about the debate.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Migration is the movement of people between places; push factors drive people to leave, while pull factors attract them to a destination. The UK has a long history of both immigration and emigration.
  • Refugees have fled persecution and are granted legal protection; asylum seekers have applied for refugee status and are awaiting a decision. Both are distinct from economic migrants and from illegal entry. Applying for asylum is a legal right under the 1951 UN Refugee Convention.
  • Immigration policy is a contested political debate: supporters highlight economic and cultural contributions, while critics raise concerns about public service pressures and integration. Students must present both viewpoints fairly and use precise citizenship terminology.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes an asylum seeker?
A) A person who has been granted refugee status after fleeing persecution
B) A person who has moved to the UK voluntarily for work
C) A person who has applied for refugee status and is awaiting a decision
D) A person who has entered the UK without a visa
practice_questions.marks: C) A person who has applied for refugee status and is awaiting a decision [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two push factors that may cause people to leave their home country.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each clearly distinct push factor, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: conflict or war; political persecution; poverty or lack of economic opportunity; environmental disaster or climate change; lack of access to education or healthcare. Two versions of the same factor (e.g. 'poverty' and 'lack of money') score only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the distinction between a refugee and an economic migrant matters in a democratic society.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. A single fully developed point with cause and consequence can score 3-4 marks.

Acceptable points include:
- Refugees have a legal right to protection under the 1951 UN Refugee Convention (point); conflating them with economic migrants could lead to people with valid protection claims being turned away, which would violate international law (consequence).
- Democratic governments have a legal obligation to process asylum claims fairly (point); accurate terminology allows citizens and policymakers to have an informed debate about immigration that does not misrepresent the status of different groups (development).
- The Equality Act 2010 and Human Rights Act 1998 protect the rights of all people in the UK, including asylum seekers (point); applying the wrong label can obscure which legal protections apply (consequence).

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

A fictional civic research institute published a report in 2024: "An analysis of tax and public spending records found that migrants who arrived in the UK aged 18-40 contributed on average £3,200 more per year in taxes than they received in public services during their first decade of residence. However, local authorities in three of the five regions studied reported increased demand for primary school places and GP appointments."

What does the extract suggest about the impact of immigration on the UK? Use the extract and your own knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for accurately identifying what the source shows (migrants make a net positive tax contribution overall but create localised pressure on specific public services); 1 mark for interpreting the significance (the impact of immigration is mixed and depends on which measure is used; national economic benefit does not automatically translate into local service capacity); 1 mark for using own knowledge to develop the point (e.g. the economic contribution of the Windrush generation to the NHS; or the policy distinction between national fiscal impact and local government funding); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement (e.g. the source suggests that the debate about immigration's impact needs to distinguish between national economic effects and local service pressures, and that both need to be addressed by policy).

practice_questions.text:
A town council is debating whether to increase funding for an integration programme for newly arrived migrants in the area. A local business association supports it; a residents' group raises concerns about the cost.

Discuss whether governments should invest more in supporting the integration of migrants into local communities.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced two-sided discussion using connectives. Arguments for investment might include: integration programmes improve social cohesion, reduce tensions and help migrants contribute economically more quickly; naming specific examples such as English language programmes or community centres is rewarded. Arguments against might include: limited public budgets mean other priorities such as schools or NHS services compete for the same funds; some argue integration should be the responsibility of communities and individuals rather than government. Names at least one specific law or institution. Reaches a substantiated position.

Secure (5-6 marks): Both perspectives present, broadly accurate, at least one named reference. Connectives used.

Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points on at least one side; limited development; no named example.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic statements; largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
A national charity that supports refugees argues: 'The UK has a moral and legal duty to accept more refugees than it currently does.'

Evaluate whether the UK has both a moral and a legal duty to accept more refugees.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Full two-sided argument. Arguments in favour might include: the 1951 UN Refugee Convention obligates signatories to assess asylum claims and protect those with a well-founded fear of persecution; the Human Rights Act 1998 incorporates the right to life and protection from inhuman treatment; the UK historically has a tradition of offering refuge (Huguenots, Jewish refugees from Eastern Europe, Windrush generation). Arguments against might include: the Convention does not specify how many refugees any country must accept, only that claims must be assessed fairly; democratic governments have a responsibility to manage borders in response to public concerns about housing and public service capacity; some argue that stronger action to address the root causes of displacement (poverty, conflict) is a more effective long-term solution than increased refugee resettlement alone. Substantiated conclusion states which consideration is most persuasive and why.

Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present, at least one named legal instrument or historical example per side. Conclusion present.

Developing (4-6 marks): Relevant points but one-sided or underdeveloped. Some real-world reference. Conclusion thin.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic statements. Largely descriptive. No substantiated judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Under which international agreement is applying for asylum a legal right?
Factors that drive people to leave their home country, such as conflict or poverty, are known as _____ factors.
When the UK left the EU in January 2020, freedom of _____ between the UK and EU member states came to an end.
Match each term to its correct definition:
right: A person granted protection after fleeing persecution
A person awaiting a decision on their protection claim
A condition that drives people to leave their home country

flashcard_questions.a: The difference between the number of people entering and leaving a country in a given period.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a push factor in migration?
flashcard_questions.a: A condition that drives people to leave their home country, such as conflict or poverty.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a pull factor in migration?
flashcard_questions.a: A condition that attracts people to a destination, such as higher wages or political safety.
A person who has fled persecution and been granted protection in another country.
A person who has applied for refugee status and is awaiting a decision.

flashcard_questions.q: What international agreement establishes the right to seek asylum?
What changed about EU citizens' right to live in the UK after January 2020?
flashcard_questions.a: Freedom of movement ended; EU citizens now need to meet points-based immigration criteria.

flashcard_questions.q: Which generation of migrants is named after a ship that arrived at Tilbury in 1948?
Give one economic argument in favour of immigration.
flashcard_questions.a: Migrants fill skills shortages in sectors such as the NHS and social care.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one concern critics raise about high levels of immigration.
flashcard_questions.a: Pressure on public services such as schools and housing in areas of high arrival.

flashcard_questions.q: What system replaced EU freedom of movement for workers in the UK?
flashcard_questions.a: A points-based immigration system applied equally to EU and non-EU citizens.

glossary_terms.definition: The movement of people from one place to another, either within a country (internal migration) or between countries (international migration).
People who move to a country other than their country of birth or citizenship in order to settle there.
People who leave their home country to settle elsewhere.
The difference between the number of people entering a country and the number leaving it in a given year.
Factors that drive people to leave their home country or region, such as poverty, conflict, persecution or lack of opportunity.
Factors that attract people to a destination country, such as higher wages, political stability, family connections or better public services.
A person who has been forced to flee their home country because of war, persecution or natural disaster and is seeking protection in another country.
A person who has applied for refugee status in another country and is waiting for a decision on whether they will be granted protection.

items.title: Newscast — BBC Sounds
items.description: BBC's impartial daily news podcast — find episodes covering UK immigration policy, asylum debates, and migration statistics from both sides of the argument.

items.title: More or Less — BBC Radio 4
items.description: Tim Harford's podcast examining the numbers behind the news — invaluable for understanding what immigration statistics actually mean versus how they are reported.

items.title: What Does It Mean to Be a Refugee? — TED-Ed
items.description: A clear, neutral explanation of the legal definition of a refugee under the 1951 UN Convention — essential for understanding the key terminology in this lesson.

items.title: He Named Me Malala (2015)
items.description: The documentary of Malala Yousafzai, a refugee and human rights campaigner — shows the human reality behind the term 'forced migration' and the right to seek asylum.

items.title: Years and Years (2019 series)
items.description: A BBC near-future drama following a British family through a turbulent decade — one storyline follows a character seeking asylum in the UK, exploring contemporary immigration debates with nuance.

items.title: UNHCR UK — Who Is a Refugee?
items.description: The UN Refugee Agency's UK site explains the 1951 Convention, the difference between refugees and asylum seekers, and global displacement data.

items.title: Full Fact — How We Fact Check Immigration
items.description: The UK's leading independent fact-checking organisation — check immigration claims you encounter in the media against the actual evidence.
